A103.text:
Registros hackeados de la agencia rusa oficial de estadísticas, Rosstat, dan por primera vez una imagen basada en datos rusos y no occidentales del costo humano de la agresión rusa contra Ucrania. Los datos, obtenidos por una organización de la oposición bielorrusa llamada ‘Cyber Partisans’ y por la organización ucraniana ‘Silent Crow’, aseguran que en Ucrania, desde el 23 de febrero de 2022, el día de la invasión, murieron al menos 392.700 soldados rusos.
Esos datos son incompletos y las cifras reales están más cerca de los 450.000 porque ahí no se cuentan ni los desaparecidos, ni los muertos cuyos cuerpos no fueron recuperados ni quienes, heridos en Ucrania, murieron de vuelta en Rusia. La información más creíble hasta ahora, que recopilaban el medio independiente ruso y el servicio ruso de la BBC, da una cifra menor de 300.000 muertos, pero explica que sólo registra los casos de los que tiene el nombre del fallecido. Las estimaciones de las organizaciones Mediazona y Meduza apuntan a unos 352.000 fallecidos. El Estado Mayor ucraniano asegura que entre muertos y heridos Rusia ha perdido ya 1,6 millones de hombres en Ucrania.
Las dos organizaciones de hackers anunciaron el 1 de noviembre que habían conseguido hackear los registros de Rosstat, accediendo a casi 25.000 computadores y a 23 terabytes de datos confidenciales. Días después, Rosstat reconoció que había sufrido ciberataques entre el 29 de octubre y el 1 de noviembre, pero aseguró que sus bases de datos no habían sido comprometidas.
La información filtrada contiene más de 11 millones de certificados de defunción de rusos desde el inicio de la guerra y lleva detalles como su lugar de residencia, su edad y su lugar de fallecimiento. De ahí se sabe cuántos murieron en Rusia. Entre el 24 de febrero de 2022 y el 30 de agosto de 2026 se registraron en esa base de datos los certificados de esas 392.700 personas muertas en Rusia. La inmensa mayoría varones. En los certificados aparecen código o anotaciones que mencionan la causa de la muerte, por ejemplo “operaciones militar”, “bombardeo” ó “drones”.
Rusia lleva desde el inicio de la guerra intentando ocultar el número real de víctimas en Ucrania y hasta ahora los datos conocidos se basaban en estimaciones de las Fuerzas Armadas ucranianas, de think tanks europeos y de los servicios secretos occidentales. Más o menos creíbles, eran datos basados en cálculos y extrapolaciones, no en los certificados de defunción. En 2015, un año después de que Rusia se hiciera por la fuerza con la provincia ucraniana de Crimea y apoyara a grupos armados prorrusos del sureste ucraniano, el presidente Vladimir Putin emitió un decreto por el que prohibía la publicación de los datos de pérdidas militares. El Gobierno ruso nunca proporcionó a su población esos datos desde que empezó la guerra.
Los datos sirven para estudiar cómo le va a Rusia en la guerra. Los registros muestran que el número de muertos aumentó drásticamente después de los primeros meses de la guerra, cuando las tropas rusas empezaron a verse bloqueadas en su avance por las ucranianas. Otros informes, estos sí de la inteligencia ucraniana y europea, muestran cómo la guerra ha tenido mayor coste humano para Rusia este año, que apenas ha avanzado sobre el terreno y que sólo el pasado octubre los rusos sufrieron, entre muertos y heridos graves, 54.000 bajas.
La guerra está teniendo un impacto enorme en la sociedad rusa. El Ejército ruso que invadió Ucrania era relativamente joven. Casi cinco años después es un ejército mucho más envejecido. La guerra apenas mataba hombres mayores en 2022 porque apenas había hombres mayores en el frente. En sus primeros seis meses sólo murieron 146 hombres de entre 50 y 59 años. En los mismos primeros meses de 2025 murieron 12.600 hombres en esa franja de edad.
La guerra tampoco afecta por igual a todas las regiones rusas.
[truncated]

A111.text:
South Africa’s young athletes have made their mark at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games, collecting nine medals so far, including two gold, as the competition makes its debut on African soil.
The Games, which run from 31 October to 13 November, are the first Olympic sporting event to be hosted on the African continent. Initially scheduled for 2022, they were postponed by four years due to the Covid-19 pandemic.
Prior to these Games, the nation’s best return was the nine medals won at the inaugural Youth Olympics in Singapore 2010. In the 2018 Buenos Aires Games, SA returned with five, while its campaign in Nanjing in 2014 yielded just one.
On 9 November, SA’s young stars added to their medal tally through athletics, with Matao le Roux clinching gold in the high jump while Enrique Bosch won the bronze in the 110m hurdles and Darius Botha secured bronze in shot put.
This puts SA tied for fifth in the overall standings with France, and 12th on the medal table when ranked by medal colour.
For many of the South African athletes in Dakar, the competition has provided an opportunity to test themselves against athletes from outside the African continent for the first time.
It has exposed them to a different level of competition as they come up against powerhouse sporting nations including China, the United States of America, Japan, France and Russia – who have been partially allowed to return to international competitions.
John-Pierre Theron, who claimed silver in the boys’ hammer throw with a distance of 71.79m, said competing internationally for the first time brought a level of pressure unlike anything he had previously experienced.
The Grade 11 learner at Hoërskool Vaaldriehoek finished narrowly behind Ecuador’s Ivan Patry Valdez Arroyo, who threw 73.27m.
“This has been amazing. To represent my country and win a medal for the team means more than I can explain,” he said.
“This was my first time competing in an international event and the level of pressure was so much higher than anything I have experienced before. I handled it well and it is a great sign of what can be achieved in the future.”
Le Roux and Dreyer strike gold
Last night, Le Roux cleared 2.16m to clinch gold in the high jump. The teenager had been under pressure after struggling to clear the heights of 2.12m and 2.14m, but responded when it mattered most.
Going head-to-head with Chinese athlete Sen Liu, Le Roux cleared 2.16m on the first attempt, leaving Liu without answers.
“I am so happy with my performance. I was really struggling with my first three jumps, and I was being put under immense pressure,” said Le Roux. “On the fourth jump I decided enough was enough and I went to put the pressure on him. I got into the groove and it flowed from there.”
Le Roux hopes the medal will create opportunities for him and his family.
“Thank you to everyone who has supported me on this journey, Team South Africa, my friends and my family, especially my mother. The two of us have been struggling for a long time and I hope this medal brings us opportunities we never had before. I want to push on from here and win more medals for my country, and for her,” he said.
Le Roux became SA’s second gold medallist at the Games, the first being the rower Callum Dreyer.
The 16-year-old turned an unfamiliar discipline to Youth Olympic gold in rowing’s coastal beach sprints solo competition. Coastal beach sprints, which combines running on the beach with rowing out to sea and back, made its Youth Olympic debut in Dakar. Dreyer became the inaugural men’s solo champion.
Dreyer had never competed in the discipline before arriving in Dakar, but quickly found his feet, winning the quarterfinals, semi-finals and the final in succession.
The Hilton College learner, who only began his rowing journey just 15 months ago, defeated Spain’s Diego Molina Martinez in the final, clocking 2:15.65 to finish 28 seconds ahead of his opponent.

A124.text:
Former South African president Kgalema Motlanthe has again urged law enforcers to go after “the big boys” of illicit narco trafficking instead of their clients, drug users.
He was speaking at a conference in Cape Town on Monday, 9 November 2026, as chair of the Eastern and Southern Africa Commission on Drugs (ESACD).
The conference was angled around the theme, “rethinking current policy responses to drug use and personal possession”.
Time for change
Delegates described an “illicit drug world” that had transformed, and emphasised the need for policies and actions to be adapted to respond to this criminal threat.
The commission was formally launched in 2023 to help in the fight against drug trafficking.
The organisation has since pushed for law enforcers to focus on narcotraffickers instead of criminalising drug users, who need better support.
The commission’s conference in Cape Town runs over two days (the first day on Monday was open to the media) at a time when shifting trafficking patterns have become more apparent in South Africa.
SA is now a transit, consumption and production hub of illicit drugs, with several massive methamphetamine (tik) factories with alleged links to Mexican cartels recently being uncovered here.
Sources in law enforcement, who have spoken to Daily Maverick on condition of anonymity, said they were worried that top drug traffickers, many probably based in other countries, were not being arrested, whereas their local foot soldiers were.
Another concern they raised with Daily Maverick is that police were also not managing to arrest those who were part of the drug manufacturing process, ranging from complicit chemical producers to transporters to equipment suppliers.
This ties into the focus of the commission’s conference.
‘For decades, our policies failed’
Motlanthe, addressing the conference on Monday, said: “For decades, our policies have failed to solve the problems created by the illicit drug trade.
“In many cases, they have done more harm than good.”
He and others who spoke at Monday’s conference flagged several other issues that needed to be addressed, including:
- The rapidly growing illicit synthetic drug trade;
- The shifting drug trafficking scene with international ramifications; and
- Imprisonment of drug users, or individuals found with drugs for personal use, while traffickers continued to break the law and push out narco consignments.
Motlanthe said that punitive measures were prioritised over harm reduction – in other words, drug users were being punished instead of being helped.
More people were being jailed for drug offences, which was adding to overcrowding in prisons, while traffickers fuelling these offences continued to operate.
“A shift in approach is needed,” Motlanthe said.
He said several countries had “explored alternatives to imprisonment”.
Drug users needed rehabilitation and treatment, including access to essential medicines and pain control (to help wean them off drugs and treat health issues related to drug use), Motlanthe said.
Speaking during a break in the conference, Motlanthe again told journalists that law enforcers should target “the big boys” and trafficking honchos, as opposed to end users.
Those end users, he said, often consumed substances without knowing what was in them, and it would be beneficial to have spaces where they could find information, including what they were actually using.
‘Jail can worsen situations’
Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia told the conference that “serious responses” were needed to tackle trafficking and the harms that drugs caused.
Law enforcement sources have told Daily Maverick that aside from potential corruption in their ranks, stretched police resources in South Africa left them feeling as if they could not fully respond to trafficking issues.

A150.text:
Mutmaßlicher Menschenhandel Viktor Orbáns Bruder offenbar festgenommen
Der Bruder von Ungarns früherem rechtsnationalistischen Regierungschef Viktor Orbán ist nach Angaben von dessen proeuropäischem Nachfolger Péter Magyar wegen des Verdachts auf Menschenhandel festgenommen worden. Magyar gab die Festnahme von Áron Orbán unter Berufung auf »Medienberichte« bekannt . Zuerst hatte die Website »Kontroll« berichtet, die Magyars Bruder gehört. Viktor Orbán sprach von einer »Hexenjagd« und einem »schmutzigen Spiel« seines Nachfolgers gegen politische Gegner, dessen eigentliches Ziel er sei.
Ein Polizeisprecher erklärte, in Budapest und zwei weiteren Städten in der Region Pest seien im Zuge von Ermittlungen im Zusammenhang mit Menschenhandel »mehrere Menschen« festgenommen worden. Die Wohnhäuser der Festgenommenen würden durchsucht.
Durchsuchtes Wohnhaus von Áron Orbán
Foto: AFP
Der frühere Regierungschef Orbán warf Magyars Regierung vor, sie wolle politische Gegner ausschalten. »Ich bin das Ziel; mein Bruder ist nur das Werkzeug«, erklärte Viktor Orbán in Onlinediensten .
Der Einsatz wurde von der unter anderem für Menschenhandel zuständigen Nationalen Ermittlungsbehörde (NNI) in Zusammenarbeit mit der neu geschaffenen Antikorruptionsbehörde NVVH ausgeführt. Diese wurde in diesem Jahr geschaffen und hat weitreichende Befugnisse. Im September hatte die NVVH laut Medienberichten vier Fälle übernommen, darunter einen wegen mutmaßlicher Einflussnahme, in die Áron Orbán verwickelt sein könnte.
Im vergangenen Jahr hatten Investigativjournalisten eins von Áron Orbán Unternehmen mit einem mutmaßlichen Visabeschaffungsprogramm in Verbindung gebracht, das ausländischen Staatsangehörigen einen bevorzugten Zugang zu ungarischen Arbeitsvisa verschafft haben soll. Áron Orbán baute wie andere Mitglieder seiner Familie während der Regierungszeit von Viktor Orbán erfolgreich Geschäftsprojekte auf.
Magyars proeuropäische Tisza-Partei hatte die Parlamentswahl im April klar gewonnen und Orbán nach 16 Jahren an der Regierung abgelöst. Magyar kündigte nach seinem Amtsantritt Ermittlungen wegen mutmaßlicher Korruption und Machtmissbrauchs unter der Führung Orbáns an. Drei ehemalige Minister wurden seither festgenommen, darunter der frühere Wirtschaftsminister und Ex-Zentralbankchef György Matolcsy, der als Orbáns »rechte Hand« galt.

A159.text:
EU seeks to pick new ECB head by year end: Eurogroup chief said
November 9, 2026
The European Union (EU) wants to name the next head of the European Central Bank by the end of the year, Eurogroup chief Kyriakos Pierrakakis said Monday.
Christine Lagarde, who has headed the ECB for seven years, announced on October 29 that she is stepping down from the position prematurely, nine months before the end of her term.
Lagarde's decision to step down early makes the schedule tight for EU leaders because they must also fill two other seats on the ECB's Executive Board within months.
"The ambition here is that the whole process would have completed itself by the end of the year," Pierrakakis said before a Eurogroup meeting of eurozone finance ministers.
"We understand that we need to move fast. But what has traditionally happened in the past is that this was a decision driven by the leaders. Today it will be primarily an information point and the discussion," he said.
Who are the candidates?
The two candidates to replace Lagarde are former Dutch Central Bank Governor Klaas Knot and the head of the Bank for International Settlements, Pablo Hernandez de Cos from Spain.
Pierrakakis said that Dutch and Spanish ministers would present their candidates and that later on Monday he would meet with Antonio Costa, head of the European Council, which represents EU governments' heads.
The appointment process requires eurozone finance ministers to put forward a candidate, followed by a European Parliament hearing and a final decision by EU leaders.
Dutch minister says the choice needs to be 'merit based'
Spanish Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo said Hernandez de Cos was the "right person for the position," referring to his long-standing experience.
"He knows the ECB inside out. He's been leading institutions such as the Bank of Spain, such as BIS as well. A steady hand, but always a profile to be able to find consensus," he told reporters.
Dutch Finance Minister Eelco Heinen, on the other hand, said Knot was an "excellent candidate", adding: "He has a very clear understanding of the ECB mandate and he has... a lot of experience to fulfill this position."
Heinen also said countries should not see the ECB leadership contest as one between northern and southern European countries, or as an "opportunity to trade favors" on other topics such as the multi-year EU budget.
A package deal is expected
The other two seats which have to be filled are those of Isabel Schnabel, the head of the ECB's market operations, who leaves on January 3, 2027, and Chief Economist Philip Lane, whose term ends in May 2027.
The three jobs are likely to be negotiated between the main eurozone countries — France, Germany, Spain and the Netherlands — as a package, Reuters news agency said, citing officials.
The expectation is that the leaders agree on a package deal on all three positions.
"Perhaps this would facilitate things. But again, this is a decision that will be taken by the leaders at the leaders level," Pierrakakis said.
Irish Finance Minister Simon Harris, whose country holds the rotating EU presidency, said he hoped Lagarde's replacement would be chosen by December.
"It certainly makes sense to fill the vacancy as quickly as possible," he said. But it's also about getting it right and getting the right person. It's a really crucial appointment."

A2.text:
Nvidia spy scandal fuels debate over chip exports to China
US lawmakers call for tighter restrictions on chip sales amid inquiry into Nvidia CEO’s relationship with alleged spy.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s intimate relationship with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy has highlighted divisions in Washington over the export of advanced chips to China.
Huang, the head of one of the most critical firms in the global artificial intelligence race, has long been among Silicon Valley’s most powerful voices arguing against restrictions on high-end chip sales.
For years, the tech executive lobbied United States President Donald Trump to loosen export controls, finding allies in sympathetic administration figures such as David Sacks, Trump’s former AI tsar.
Whereas hawkish voices argued that Beijing should not have access to cutting-edge US technology on national security grounds, Huang and like-minded executives argued that China already had the computing power to make strides in AI and that wider uptake of US technology would help maintain its dominance in the field.
Jensen Huang’s lobbying now faces intense scrutiny following claims that former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang — with whom he had an affair — was an intelligence agent recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security.
China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has denied the allegations, calling them “entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China”.
Alice Huang has not publicly commented on the claims, which The New York Times and the Financial Times first reported, citing unnamed US intelligence officials.
Nvidia’s board of directors on Sunday launched an inquiry into Jensen Huang’s relationship, pledging to examine “all available information” while also expressing confidence in the CEO.
Jensen Huang, who cofounded Nvidia in 1993, has pledged to cooperate fully with the inquiry and expressed his commitment to protecting Nvidia and US national security.
Trump has meanwhile said the FBI too is investigating whether Huang’s affair led to any compromise on US national security.
Already, US lawmakers have invoked the controversy to push for tighter restrictions on China’s access to US chips.
Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren and Republican Senator Jim Banks on Monday called on the US Congress to take “decisive action” and pass their AI Overwatch Act, which would empower lawmakers to scrutinise and potentially halt exports of advanced chips to China and other adversaries.
“The Commerce Department should complement these efforts with immediate action to close export control loopholes and ensure that advanced AI chips are not going to China’s military,” Warren and Banks said in a joint statement.
Democratic House Representative Bill Foster also cited Jensen Huang’s relationship in a statement on Monday in which he called on his fellow lawmakers to get his Chip Security Act “across the finish line”.
The legislation, cosponsored by Republican House Representative Bill Huizenga, aims to prevent illicit smuggling to countries such as China by implementing measures to track the location of chips sent overseas.
Advocates of tighter restrictions now have a “much stronger political argument” and are likely to make use of it, said Rui Ma, a tech industry consultant and founder of Tech Buzz China.
“Chip exports to China have been deeply divisive in Washington, and Huang has been one of the strongest advocates for keeping that market open,” Ma told Al Jazeera.
“If his influence is diminished by this investigation, regardless of its eventual findings, those pushing for tighter restrictions will be in a much stronger position,” she said.
Trump, who has forged a close relationship with Jensen Huang since returning to the White House, has taken several actions to make it easier for chip makers to do business with China, while also maintaining significant export controls.

A213.text:
Details of Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO, including plans by the AI company to raise nearly US$70-billion, were briefly circulated to banks before being retracted late on Monday, according to emails seen by Reuters.
A representative of Anthropic sent a copy of a securities filing that showed it aimed to sell about 867 million shares at a price range of US$70 to US$80 per share, then followed up with an e-mail saying details about the pricing were inaccurate. Anthropic said in the second e-mail it would update the filing later.
Anthropic declined to comment. The e-mail did not specify to bankers what was erroneous, and Reuters was unable to determine what was incorrect.
The original e-mail whose details were retracted showed Anthropic planned to sell 866.7 million Class A shares, including a secondary offering. Anthropic itself would sell about 843.3 million shares, while existing shareholders would sell an additional 23.3 million shares. The IPO would raise US$69.3-billion at the top of the range.
Separately, the original filing showed that Anthropic had lined up US$26-billion in investments from some of the world’s biggest technology companies alongside its IPO, underscoring the increasingly intertwined financial ties underpinning the AI boom.
Alphabet’s Google GOOGL-Q, Nvidia NVDA-Q, Advanced Micro Devices AMD-Q, Broadcom AVGO-Q, Micron Technology MU-Q, Microsoft MSFT-Q and TSMC TSM-N had agreed to participate in the private placement of Anthropic’s Class N common stock at the IPO price, which would close immediately after the IPO, the original filing showed.
Anthropic’s IPO timing in doubt due to AI backlash, sources say
Anthropic is expected to formally launch the road show on Tuesday, with pricing expected in the following week.
The Anthropic IPO comes at a time when other companies in the AI infrastructure and data centre sectors have delayed or withdrawn their planned listings, facing a rise in interest rates that has helped fuel a punishing selloff in shares and bonds of AI operators such as CoreWeave Inc CRWV-Q and broader questions about the sustainability of AI spending.
Investors had previously discussed a valuation of as much as US$2-trillion for Anthropic, but expectations have since come down, with the US$1.5-trillion figure viewed as the high end of the range, Reuters previously reported.
Founded in 2021 by former OpenAI executives including Amodei and his sister Daniela Amodei, who is now Anthropic’s president, Anthropic has emerged as one of the leading generative AI developers with its Claude family of models.
The company’s rapid growth has been underpinned by Google and Amazon AMZN-Q, which are simultaneously investors, suppliers of computing power and important distribution partners, as well as AI competitors.
Anthropic had nearly US$900-billion in computing commitments with partners including Amazon and Google, underscoring how its rapid growth depends on vast amounts of future capacity, some of it reliant on financing beyond the company’s control.
Anthropic’s quarterly growth rate has declined sharply even though revenue stood at almost US$17-billion for the three months ended Sept. 30, the company revealed in an amended filing earlier in the month.

A22.text:
European diplomats press Rubio for a role in Russia-Ukraine talks
G7 foreign ministers are meeting in Paris ahead of the US-mediated Russia-Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi.
European foreign ministers have told United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio that Europe must have a say in any deal to end Russia’s war on Ukraine, as US-mediated peace talks get under way in Abu Dhabi.
They made the appeal on Monday in Paris, at a meeting of foreign ministers from the Group of Seven, which includes Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States.
It was Rubio’s first meeting with allies since last week’s midterm elections, in which President Donald Trump’s Republican Party suffered stunning losses. The meeting gave Washington’s allies a chance to air their concerns with Rubio directly amid concern about Trump’s growing rhetoric of a new security architecture for Europe.
“It is certainly neither necessary, nor right, nor appropriate to make a fundamental change” to Europe’s security architecture, said German Minister for Foreign Affairs Johann Wadephul after talks with Rubio.
“Europe belongs at this table. There can be no solution without Europe – only with Europe,” he added.
The two-day Paris meeting, which ends on Tuesday, overlaps with the talks between Russia and Ukraine, scheduled for Tuesday and Wednesday.
Wadephul said the Abu Dhabi talks must show whether Russia is “genuinely prepared to negotiate”, urging Moscow to “give up maximalist demands” and warning against any “negotiation show” in the capital of the United Arab Emirates.
With Russian attacks on Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure continuing, he said, “we see no substantial contribution whatsoever toward negotiations gaining any serious momentum” from Moscow.
Andrii Sybiha, Ukraine’s foreign minister, is set to join a session on Ukraine in Paris on Tuesday.
“No one has the right to decide our fate behind our backs,” Sybiha said before departing for the meeting.
The Paris meeting comes as G7 members have grown increasingly uneasy with the direction of US policy, including Washington’s scaling back of support for Ukraine and of sanctions on Russia, as well as its increasingly unilateral course.
Ministers from Saudi Arabia, Egypt, South Korea and Brazil are also attending.
Iran is expected to feature prominently in the discussions on Tuesday.
Washington’s G7 allies have repeatedly voiced scepticism about the US and Israeli war on Iran and fear that further US military action could deepen the crisis rather than resolve it.
Al Jazeera’s Rebecca Collard, reporting from Paris, said the first day of talks had wrapped up with little clarity on US policy after the midterm elections.
“The second day of talks will include a session on instability in the Middle East,” she said.
“But there is something bigger up for discussion, too: The future of the multilateralism that has dominated relations among these countries for decades.”

A24.text:
Saudi Arabia downs missiles fired at Riyadh after Houthi attack on pipeline
Saudi forces intercept two missiles fired towards Riyadh, hours after reporting damage to key East-West pipeline.
The Saudi Arabia-led coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis has announced it intercepted two missiles fired towards the kingdom’s capital, Riyadh, and another aimed at its southern region.
Major-General Turki al-Maliki, a spokesperson for the coalition, blamed the Iran-backed Houthis for Tuesday’s attacks.
In a series of posts on X, he said a ballistic missile and a cruise missile were intercepted and destroyed over Riyadh, while a second ballistic missile was downed over the southern part of the country.
Multiple explosions were heard in Riyadh, according to the AFP news agency, and residents received text-message alerts instructing them to take shelter due to an “aerial threat”.
A subsequent message from the country’s civil defence agency said the danger had passed.
There was no immediate comment from the Houthis.
Meanwhile, the Houthi-run Saba news agency reported Saudi-led coalition air strikes on Sanaa, the Yemeni capital, which the Houthis control.
Saba said the strikes hit the al-Mufazir gas facility in the Jadar district, north of the capital, and a building belonging to the state oil company in southern Sanaa. Civil defence teams were working to put out a fire in gas trailers at the al-Mufazir station, it said.
The coalition did not immediately confirm the strikes.
The attacks were the latest in a series of exchanges as fighting rages in Yemen between the Houthis and the country’s internationally recognised government, which is backed by Riyadh.
The Saudi-led coalition has supported a Yemeni government offensive to retake territory with air strikes, while the Houthis have repeatedly struck Saudi oil infrastructure, including refineries and storage facilities, with drones and missiles.
On Monday, the East-West oil pipeline in Saudi Arabia’s Medina region was attacked again. A Saudi Ministry of Energy official told the state-run SPA news agency the strike caused a “limited fire” that was extinguished. The official said that “pipeline operations were unaffected”.
No injuries or deaths were reported.
The pipeline is a vital route for Saudi oil exports due to Tehran’s restrictions in the Strait of Hormuz following the US-Israel war against Iran. The pipeline has come under attack several times, as the war on Iran fuels a global energy crisis.
On Sunday, the Houthis also said they attacked Riyadh’s business district.
Saudi officials said falling debris from an “attempted attack” had caused minor damage to the Aramco Tower.
Images released by the SPA showed the deputy governor of the Riyadh region and other officials inspecting the building, with damage visible on several floors.

Benjamin Netanyahu remains Israel's prime minister when the new parliament takes office Tuesday but its new, less friendly composition could make his life much more difficult.
Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief seeking to move Israel to the centre, was given the mandate Sunday by President Isaac Herzog to form a new government, a complicated task as neither he nor Netanyahu command a majority.
Until then Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving leader, remains caretaker prime minister -- but the new 120-member parliament can still go to battle against him.
The lack of a new government "does not infringe upon the Knesset's prerogatives", said Assaf Shapira, a political expert at the Israel Democracy Institute.
Eisenkot has also warned military chiefs that Netanyahu does not have a mandate to resume war against Iran -- although the statement was more about politics than the law, with Netanyahu still in charge of national security.
Netanyahu's bloc slipped to 53 seats in the new parliament, down from the decisive 68 it commanded previously.
Eisenkot's core opposition bloc has fewer seats than Netanyahu at 48 but the new parliament also has a record 19 lawmakers from Arab-majority parties that are vehemently opposed to Netanyahu and his hard-right government -- although it remains unclear if Eisenkot will seek to work with Israeli-Arabs directly.
Here are ways in which the new parliament could turn on Netanyahu:
- Commission on October 7 attacks -
One of the opposition's main campaign promises has been to set up a commission of inquiry to probe failures in the famously high-security country that allowed Hamas's October 7, 2023, attack, the deadliest ever day for Israel.
While Netanyahu denies any wrongdoing on his part, his government has consistently opposed the creation of a national, independent commission of inquiry that would have broad investigative authority, with Netanyahu instead supporting a review by political appointees.
Even before a new government is formed, the incoming parliament could set up a special committee on the attack which would hand over its findings to an eventual commission of inquiry, Shapira said.
Eisenkot declared after the election that forming a commission would be an immediate priority.
- Repealing Netanyahu-era laws -
The new parliament could also move quickly to repeal some of the most controversial laws under Netanyahu, including his efforts to revamp the judiciary -- seen by the prime minister as an enemy after he was charged with corruption.
The judicial revamp triggered some of Israel's largest ever protests, with liberals worried about the future of democracy, although the Hamas attack and subsequent wars quickly shifted public attention.
The new parliament could aim to repeal the last coalition's laws that limited the powers of the Supreme Court and made it easier to remove the country's attorney general.
Lawmakers could also roll back exemptions for ultra-Orthodox Jews from serving in the military. The exemption has angered many Israelis at a time that the military is stretched thin, although the laws did not go far enough for ultra-Orthodox parties, who are being wooed by at least one opposition figure.
Shapira said repealing Netanyahu-era laws was as simple as calling a vote and reverting to previous policies. But the process to pass new laws could take weeks as the opposition coordinates its priorities.
- Electing new speaker -
The first political clash will concern electing a new parliament speaker. The incumbent is Amir Ohana, a Netanyahu loyalist from his Likud Party.
According to parliamentary rules, the vote for speaker can take place as early as during the inaugural session and must happen before a new government is sworn in.

Claude Code is leaking sensitive information on public GitHub instances thanks to a partial oversight in the way its settings files are handled. That’s the finding of AI security researchers at Apiiro, who discovered thousands of secrets, including database passwords, API tokens, and root logins, amid Claude Code settings files embedded in GitHub repositories.
The leak stems from the way Claude Code handles user approval for automated shell commands. When a user chooses the “Yes, and don’t ask again” option to approve running a command, that choice gets stored as part of a rule in the local “.claude/settings.local.json” file on the user’s computer. That rule is sometimes coded as a pattern, but the command itself is often written to that settings file as is, including any sensitive information that may be embedded within it.
This isn’t really a significant security issue if the settings file stays on the user’s local machine (assuming that machine doesn’t become compromised itself, of course). And Anthropic notes in its Claude Code documentation that this particular settings file gets added to the developer’s global .gitignore list, which usually prevents it from being shared publicly.
But that .gitignore setting isn’t reflected at the repo level, meaning the sensitive file can be uploaded accidentally if a repo is cloned to another machine or a folder becomes a repo later, for instance. In many cases, Claude Code itself will commit changes to the settings file without the user’s input, Apiiro writes.
Apiiro’s researchers found over 100,000 cases where Claude Code’s local settings file had been uploaded to a public GitHub repository. Of these, only about 1,100 from 63 different organizations contained secrets such as public API tokens, database passwords, or private keys. Even after these files are discovered and removed from a repository, the secrets can persist in forks of the original project if a GitHub user isn’t careful.

The Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) Fifth Plenum, held on October 26–29, offered important insights into General Secretary Xi Jinping’s evolving system of political control. Its decision on “comprehensive and strict party governance” underscores how the institutionalization of continuous political rectification has become a hallmark of Xi’s rule.
The Fifth Plenum is significant for three reasons. First, it consolidates “Xi Jinping Thought on Party Building” (XJTPB) as an authoritative framework for CCP governance. Second, it embeds continuous political rectification within the party’s governing institutions. Third, it exposes an unresolved tension between the party’s enhanced capacity to punish misconduct and the continuation of problems of political reliability, information distortion, and delegated authority.
Xi Jinping Thought on Party Building
The plenum’s communiqué identified XJTPB as an authoritative component of “Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era.” Its core contribution is to address what the CCP regards as the fundamental question of “how to build a long-term ruling Marxist party” capable of maintaining its monopoly on political power indefinitely.
XJTPB’s answer to this question is that the “political construction” of party members must take precedence over all else. This entails that all party members “uphold the party’s nature and purpose” by “strengthening ideals and beliefs” and “forging loyalty to the party.” Only in this way can party members “be loyal, clean, and responsible.” Political reliability thus becomes the indispensable qualification for advancement and the exercise of authority by party cadres.
Yet political reliability is not enough. Rather, the CCP and its individual members must be committed to “self-revolution” through the continual identification and correction of political, ideological, organizational, and disciplinary weaknesses.
This approach has historical antecedents in Mao Zedong’s Yan’an rectification movement, which linked the forging of ideological conformity and organizational discipline to the consolidation of Mao’s undisputed leadership. Unlike Mao’s subsequent episodic campaigns, however, Xi arguably seeks to institutionalize rectification as a permanent feature of party governance. Indeed, the CCP, the communique exhorted, must continually “turn the blade inward” to identify and eliminate threats arising from within its own ranks.
“Self-revolution” however also reflects a broader concern with political survival. As Neil Thomas and Shengyu Wang have argued, Xi’s interpretation of the rise and fall of Chinese dynasties and the collapse of the Soviet Union stresses the danger that even powerful ruling organizations can succumb to corruption, complacency, and internal decay. Thus, the communique explicitly identified the party’s capacity for “self-purification, self-renewal, and self-enhancement” as fundamental to its ability to “break free from the historical cycle of governance and chaos.”
XJTPB therefore does more than legitimize Xi’s authority as it supplies the normative foundations for treating supervision, discipline, and ideological correction as permanent requirements of party governance.
The Institutionalization of Rectification
The communique listed three priorities for translating these principles into institutional practice: tighter management and supervision of officials; stronger party organizations throughout the governance hierarchy; and integration of disciplinary enforcement, behavioral correction and anti-corruption measures.
[truncated]

A55.text:
Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy
- Published
US President Donald Trump has said the FBI is investigating the affair between the chief executive of Nvidia and an alleged Chinese spy.
Trump said he spoke to Jensen Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign.
"I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters.
Beijing has rejected claims that Huang was targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".
Speaking later at a White House press briefing, Trump told reporters, "I know the FBI is looking into" the affair but did not give further details on the investigation, or confirm when it was launched.
Trump added he thought that Huang was an "honourable guy and I feel very confident that he will be in good shape" after the investigations.
The FBI declined to comment when contacted by the BBC.
Nvidia, which has commissioned an independent investigation into the affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy, said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised.
Nvidia is the world's second most valuable company after Apple, and designs computer chips that have become central to AI technology.
The revelations knocked about $250bn (£190bn) off Nvidia's value on Monday as the company's share price fell by more than 4%.
US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report. She is not related to Jensen Huang.
According to the newspaper, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington in spring this year, warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.
- What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy 
  - Published10 hours ago
- Nvidia shares tumble over investigation into Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy 
  - Published14 hours ago
Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia.
Trump's remarks are the first indication of whether Nvidia's Huang knew about the woman's alleged ties to Chinese espionage.
Megaspeed's office in Singapore's central business district appeared to be operational and staffed on Tuesday.
The BBC was refused entry to its floor, but spoke to a staff member by phone who said they had no comment and directed all queries to the company's PR team.
The BBC has emailed Megaspeed several times for comment.
Nvidia, co-founded by Jensen Huang, is also a major focus in the AI technology race between the US and China, with officials in Washington treating its exports to Beijing as a matter of national security - a key reason why Huang's affair has sparked concerns.
Also on Monday, Huang and Nvidia were sued in a proposed class action lawsuit in California that accuses them of defrauding shareholders by concealing his ties with the suspected Chinese spy.
The lawsuit alleges that the company lied to the media about Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, "who is suspected of seeking to help smuggle Nvidia products to China."
The BBC has contacted Nvidia for comment on the lawsuit.
'An honourable guy'
At the White House, Trump was asked several times when he was made aware of the relationship. He said he was informed "over a period of time" but was not specific.
"I hope there's no problem, I believe he is suffering greatly," the president added.
He said he spoke to Huang on the phone on Monday "just to see if he's feeling alright, how you doing and I asked him about that and he said he absolutely had no idea that the person in question was a spy".

A590.text:
Europe’s manufacturers could give up on attempting to compete with their Chinese counterparts by the end of the decade if current trends continue amid fears over mass job losses, the head of the European Union Chamber of Commerce in China has warned.
In a case of “if you can’t beat them, join them”, Jens Eskelund said European companies operating in China were now thinking “Made in China for China” could be replaced by a philosophy of “Made in China for the world”.
Eskelund, who heads the influential Beijing-headquartered body, said European manufacturers could find themselves at an existential crossroads by the end of the decade, asking themselves: “What is the point of trading?”
As the EU gets tough with China with a deficit running at a record £1bn (€1.18bn) a day and an increasing mood for protectionism in Brussels, Berlin and Paris, he said European countries might need to shift their policies to allow domestic manufacturers to become part of Chinese firms’ supply chains, rather than treat them as competitors.
Eskelund, who is also a managing director of the shipping group Maersk’s Chinese operations, pointed to a report by Goldman Sachs that forecasted Chinese exports would lower the EU’s gross domestic product by 0.5% by the end of the decade while reducing Germany’s by up to 0.9%.
“It raises the question, if China’s trade delivers negative value, why trade?” the Danish businessman said.
“If you are suddenly in a situation where trade creates a lot of value for one party, but it destroys value for the other, countries will begin to ask themselves, why do we trade?” he said, pointing to a potential doomsday scenario in which manufacturing disappeared from European countries, causing mass job losses, collapse in the tax base and potential multigenerational unemployment and spiralling social benefits costs.
Speaking in Brussels, where he has been in back-to-back meetings with European Commission officials to give them feedback from Beijing, he said Europe is at an inflection point.
“If we create new dependencies, ultimately that might result in Europe losing its ability to determine its own future,” with mass job losses and fraying of communities, Eskelund added.
That existential threat is already beginning to bite in Europe’s car, chemicals and renewable energy sectors, with the German automotive industry hit by a double whammy of reduced profits in China and cheap competition at home from Chinese companies such as BYD, Geely and SAIC Motor. Last week, BMW said its sales in China had dropped 22% in the first nine months of the year, in line with expectations of suppressed domestic demand, while issuing a second profit warning this year.
Eskelund is not a fan of the term “China shock 2.0” – which refers to the impact of the huge rise in exports of, cars, chemicals and components – on local industry to the EU in the last five years. He said it should not have come as a surprise as Beijing’s plans to displace imports were the enduring theme of the last three five-year plans since Beijing’s Made in China strategy was agreed in 2015.
“I don’t really like the term China shock 2.0 because these things that are happening should not be a shock because it is all written in their five-year plans so you should be able to anticipate that,” Eskelund said.
“The proof of concept here is that China has been laser-focused on reducing its own dependencies over the last 30 years,” he added, pointing to a concomitant reduction in imports.
A recent report by Centre for European Reform (CER) urged Germany to stop “admiring” Beijing and change its strategy, with China’s latest five-year plan (2026 to 2030) a doubling-down on “self-reliance”.
“It is committed to displacing imports in the few sectors where it still depends on foreign supply,” said the CER.
[truncated]

A64.text:
Australia considers criminal penalties for rogue AI in wake of OpenAI hack
- Published
Australia plans to create a new AI safety regulator and has flagged criminal penalties for tech companies who do not comply, months after an OpenAI hack.
In September, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed that a rogue OpenAI agent had "infiltrated" a government health website and other systems, and criticised the company for taking months to tell them about the hack.
On Tuesday, he released the 18 recommendations made after a "rapid review" into the breaches including new safety and security standards for AI companies such as mandatory reporting of hacks.
AI brings opportunities, he said, but Australia must prepare for the "new risks" from this "rapidly advancing technology".
"The law needs to get ahead of and, in some cases, make sure that it catches up with, what is a very fast changing world," Albanese said.
One of the recommendations suggests changes to criminal law to have a standalone "failure to prevent" offence .
This would criminalise instances where a company develops "an AI model that engages in harmful conduct" and "fails to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm".
The review also recommended "mandatory, time-bound AI safety reporting" of hacks.
This point addresses what Albanese had earlier called his "disappointment" in the months-long delay for OpenAI to tell his government about the breach.
In June, a statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare was hacked by a rogue OpenAI agent.
OpenAI said it only learnt of the breach in August while reviewing "misaligned model activity" and emailed a general inbox of an Australian government agency on 10 September.
It took several more days before the email was escalated to Australia's cybersecurity centre, with a message then sent to a government minister ahead of the prime minister being told.
Albanese said he spoke to OpenAI boss Sam Altman and raised "Australia's extreme concern about this incident", with Altman acknowledging there were "issues with protocols" at OpenAI.
Days after the hacks were revealed, OpenAI delayed its rollout of a new AI model, citing safety concerns.

A65.text:
France accuses Iran of supermarket fridge hacking
- Published
France has accused Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of being behind cyber-attacks that raised the temperatures of supermarket fridges and freezers across the country last month.
Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said the attack was "unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression", adding those who were responsible would be hit with sanctions.
Iran has yet to respond officially, but some Iranian media outlets have dismissed the allegations as baseless.
The French hacking, which led to the destruction of tons of frozen and chilled food in France was followed by a similar attack against supermarkets across several other European countries. It is not known if the instances are linked.
Barrot said the attack on France's supermarkets "marks the first large-scale cyber-attack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation's interests and the security of the French people".
He said the government had summoned the Iranian ambassador to Paris to "lodge a very strong protest against this extremely grave act".
France will take "any other necessary and proportionate measures" to respond to the incident and "deter anyone who might seek to repeat it", Barrot added.
The Paris prosecutor said an investigation had been opened into the head of an offensive cyber unit associated with the IRGC as well as his two deputies.
Laure Beccuau named the unit as Shahid Kaveh, which she said had an affiliation with the electronic and cyber centre of the IRGC.
Shahid Kaveh is the name given to a cluster of hackers thought to be directly employed by the Iranian regime.
In recent weeks, a number of commentators and politicians in Iran have argued that the country should extend any retaliation beyond the Middle East if the US and Israel resume the war they started earlier this year.
If the IRGC carried out the cyber-attacks, it remains unclear whether they were part of Iran's deterrence strategy.
On 11 October, hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units used in many of France's supermarkets.
More than 100 of Coopérative U's supermarkets were hit, as well as 180 stores from Intermarché and its Netto brand. In some stores, temperatures of the fridges reportedly rose to 50C (120F) overnight.
Other major food retailers including Carrefour, Monoprix and E.Leclerc were also hit by the attack, which targeted software provided by Danish engineering firm Danfoss.
The software allows retailers to manage their cold units remotely.
Earlier this month a second wave of hacks took place, hitting more than 100 stores across Europe.
Supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in countries including Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.
Separately in August a small number of US military bases had fridges mysteriously malfunction, spoiling food. This incident is also being investigated as deliberate cyber-attacks, Reuters news agency has reported, citing sources familiar with the matter.
Since the waves of attacks on freezers, experts have been speculating which hacking groups could be responsible, with Iran being on a list of potential suspects.
In spite of a pair of Russian-aligned hacktivist groups claiming they were responsible on Wednesday, few believed them.
The French government has not said how it reached the conclusion that Iran was responsible, and attribution of cyber-attacks is extremely hard as hackers are able to hide their locations.
Additional reporting by Farshad Bayan, BBC Persian.
Related topics

A7.text:
What powers does Netanyahu have as Israel’s interim PM?
As Israel navigates political gridlock, Benjamin Netanyahu retains vast executive authority despite his caretaker status.
Two weeks after Israel’s national elections, opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has been given a chance by President Isaac Herzog to cobble together a government.
But with neither Eisenkot nor Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition securing the 61 seats needed to secure a majority in the Knesset, who eventually forms the next administration is far from clear.
As Eisenkot huddles with members of his alliance and negotiates with potential outside partners who could support his coalition, including Arab parties, Netanyahu remains ensconced as a caretaker prime minister. And if Eisenkot fails to form a government, Herzog might approach Netanyahu to see if he can form a workable coalition government.
This transitional status creates a unique political landscape where the incumbent lacks a popular mandate but retains the keys to the state’s most powerful institutions.
“Netanyahu lost the priority of forming the government, but he did not lose the current premiership,” Ehab Jabareen, an analyst and Palestinian citizen of Israel, told Al Jazeera. “His power now lies in that his opponents need an agreement to remove him – and their differences are the reason for his current [political] survival.”
In the meantime, Jabareen explained, Israel sits in a “constitutional paradox”: The prime minister does not enjoy a popular mandate.
So what does that mean for Israel, and what powers does Netanyahu enjoy as a caretaker prime minister?
The big picture
Israel has no single constitution but instead relies on a series of what are known as Basic Laws as its foundational legal principles.
Under Article 30 of Israel’s Basic Law: The Government, the outgoing administration continues to operate seamlessly until there is a new one sworn in to replace it.
“Consequently, Netanyahu and his government continue to work until a new government gains the confidence of the Knesset under the principle of government continuity,” Jabareen said.
“And in this period, the government retains the powers of managing the state, security and foreign relations, but its use is subject to the duty of reservation and restraint.”
Security and war
The most pressing concern surrounding Netanyahu’s caretaker status is his authority over the military.
He has the authority to make new appointments and security-related decisions. But he is expected to face extra scrutiny over any moves because while he has legal powers, he does not necessarily enjoy “legitimacy” any more, Jabareen noted.
While Netanyahu commands the executive branch, Article 40 of the Basic Law: The Government authorises his cabinet to launch a new war if it votes in its favour. He cannot start a new conflict on his own.
But Netanyahu can strategically manipulate existing conflicts. “The most applicable scenario is not inventing a war from scratch, of course. We are talking about igniting and employing an existing threat. We are talking about Iran. We are talking about Lebanon,” Jabareen said.
Because Eisenkot and his allies are not members of the current security cabinet, Netanyahu wields unchecked influence over how intelligence is framed.
“What is presented to the ministers as a danger that can be contained? And what is presented as a final opportunity [for potential attacks] that cannot be delayed? This additional responsibility of the prime minister regarding the information that reaches the cabinet makes the presentation of options extremely important,” Jabareen explained.
The Shin Bet, Israel’s internal intelligence agency, reports directly to the premier. That does not change while Netanyahu is a caretaker prime minister.
Legislative boundaries
While Netanyahu commands security forces, his domestic and legislative powers face functional limits.

A8.text:
US moves aircraft from second UK base over ‘threat from Iran’
The United States military has moved aircraft from a second airbase in the United Kingdom “in the wake of a threat from Iran”, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter.
Two US refuelling tankers and several other tankers that were using the RAF Mildenhall military base in eastern England diverted to Germany and other locations on Monday, the WSJ reported on Tuesday.
The report said the precise nature of the threat to RAF Mildenhall remains under discussion among US officials.
The US upgraded the security posture at RAF Mildenhall and RAF Lakenheath to Force Protection Condition (FPCON) Charlie, the WSJ report said, quoting a US official familiar with the matter.
FPCON Charlie is the second-highest defensive threat level in the US Department of Defense’s security system and occurs when intelligence indicates that a form of “terrorist” action is likely.
“We do not routinely comment on the activity of other nations,” a UK Ministry of Defence spokesperson said in a statement.
“Aircraft and other assets move regularly according to operational requirements.”
A US Air Force spokesperson said aircraft rotate between installations and operating locations for various reasons.
The report comes weeks after five men were arrested outside RAF Fairford airbase in southwest England over a security incident, with two others arrested later on suspicion of assisting Iranian intelligence.
The circumstances of the September incident remain largely unexplained, but it prompted the US to remove its B-1 bombers from the airbase on security grounds.
It came at a time of heightened concern about the wider security implications of the US-Israel war on Iran.
RAF Fairford had been used by US bombers that carried out strikes on Iran.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said last month that the activity at RAF Fairford was likely to have been coordinated in Iran.
While Tehran’s ambassador to the UK has denied accusations that it was involved in any plot against the airbase, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said in July that Fairford and any other base used to launch attacks against Iran were legitimate targets.

A9.text:
Australia tightens AI oversight rules after OpenAI government breach
The decision comes after an OpenAI agent breached an Australian government website in June.
Australia will make it mandatory for artificial intelligence companies to immediately report when their AI models go rogue and to open their models for evaluation, the government said.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Tuesday the government had accepted all recommendations from a rapid review into the breach, which “include mandatory AI company reporting when it comes to misaligned behaviour or cyber-incidents, and consideration of reforming criminal law in cases of serious misconduct”.
“Australia is the first mover in this space, and we want to make sure that we continue to work so that we can reap the potential benefits from AI,” he said.
The decision comes after OpenAI-powered models hacked into an Australian government health data system in June, slipping past its digital defences and accessing files without authorisation.
Top AI firms have recently raised the alarm regarding the risk of humans losing control of their systems, calling for AI development to slow down to a pace that allows it to be safely regulated.
Earlier this year, Anthropic’s safety research scientist Evan Hubinger went so far as to say he believes there is a greater than 10 percent chance that AI could “kill all humans” within a decade.
Rapid incident notifications
The new Australian AI regulator will oversee security controls throughout the development and deployment of AI systems, identify and manage serious risks, and conduct independent evaluations of AI models.
The AI standards would also mandate rapid notification to the government of incidents such as “misaligned behaviour” conflicting with developers’ intentions.
Australian government documents define frontier AI as the most sophisticated models at the cutting edge of current technological capability.
Albanese told OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman that the US company took too long to inform the government of the incident. OpenAI apologised for the breach and its slow response.
Inquiry recommends law changes
A government inquiry into the June breach made several recommendations, including that the government consider changing the law.
The proposed AI regulator would follow Australia’s appointment of an eSafety Commissioner in 2015. The office describes itself as the world’s first government agency dedicated to keeping people safer online.
Since December last year, the commissioner has been enforcing a world-first ban on Australian children younger than 16 holding accounts on popular social media platforms.

A120.text:
By Steve Holland, Courtney Rozen, Karen Freifeld and David Shepardson
Trump said he “was amazed” by allegations about Huang, among the president’s closest allies in Silicon Valley. Trump said he had spoken to the CEO, who told him that he had no idea that the woman was a spy.
“I know the FBI is looking into it,” Trump said. “I think that he'll be in good shape,” he added.
Nvidia shares closed down more than 4% on Monday after the company's board launched an internal investigation into whether Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort.
The probe, announced on Sunday, has put a spotlight on 63-year-old Huang's future given Nvidia's status as the world's most valuable chipmaker and the CEO's role as the most prolific salesman of the AI boom. Huang told Nvidia's employees that he had been unfaithful to his wife, without disclosing details of the relationship.
The leather-jacketed Huang enjoys rock-star status worldwide, particularly in Asia, where he often mingles freely with fans, taking selfies and signing autographs for his devoted followers.
He is Nvidia's fifth-largest shareholder with a roughly 3.6% stake, according to LSEG data, and keeps a tight grip on the company through an unusually flat structure in which dozens of executives report directly to him.
But unlike Mark Zuckerberg's Meta Platforms META.O or Elon Musk's SpaceX SPCX.O, Nvidia has no dual-class shares that would give co-founder Huang majority voting control.
The New York Times reported that Trump was briefed on Huang's relationship with the woman and that she was giving information to the Chinese government, and that the president chose not to act on the information.
"The so-called Chinese spy narrative is purely a groundless accusation, slander, and a smear," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters in Beijing.
Huang's relationship with Trump has coincided with several favorable policy developments for the company, and the president has lavished Huang with praise, awarding him the nation's highest honor for scientific achievement in October.
The same day Trump gave Huang the award, the president disclosed buying up to $1.6 million and selling up to $1 million of Nvidia shares during the summer.
'NOT AN ORDINARY CEO'
Nvidia said its board has confidence in Huang, thought by many on Wall Street to be the most important person underpinning the AI trade. Analysts acknowledged uncertainty around succession, but most do not expect the investigation to result in the longtime CEO stepping down.
"Nvidia is not an ordinary company and Jensen is not an ordinary CEO; he is Nvidia, clearly sets the long-term strategy and direction, and pulls most of the company's strings himself," said Stacy Rasgon, an analyst at Bernstein.
Nvidia shareholders were quick to sue Huang and the company in a proposed class action on Monday, accusing them of defrauding shareholders by concealing Huang's ties with a suspected Chinese spy.
Lawmakers and advocates told Reuters that Congress was more likely to pass legislation to tighten China's access to AI chips in light of news of Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence agent.
US House of Representatives Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said on Monday that Congress needs more answers and called for the House to pass an annual defense bill that includes restrictions on chip sales to China.
The New York Times reported last month that Huang had a relationship with Alice Huang, an unrelated former executive of Singapore-based company Megaspeed, who US authorities investigated and concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset.
Megaspeed did not respond immediately to a request for comment on Monday, a public holiday in Singapore.
Alice Huang did not respond to the New York Times last month when it first reported her relationship with Huang, and Reuters could not determine her location to seek comment on Monday.
[truncated]

A126.text:
By Steve Holland and Humeyra Pamuk
The official, briefing reporters ahead of talks that begin on Tuesday, said security guarantees for Ukraine will be a major topic for the discussions, including the potential for a NATO-style Article 5 defense for Kyiv.
Both Ukraine and Russia have been adamant about territory. Ukraine wants Russia pushed back to the original border between the two countries, while Russian President Vladimir Putin wants to obtain all of the Donbas region.
But the official said both sides are privately showing some potential for a compromise. Any territorial agreement would likely come at the end of negotiations once other items are agreed upon, including a postwar security architecture, the official said.
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are to lead US mediation efforts in the Abu Dhabi talks, which are scheduled for two days. The official said it was possible the envoys would travel to Russia at some point after the talks in order to meet with Putin.
While noting that the negotiations would take some time, the official said there was cautious optimism on the US side that progress can be made.
Trump has repeatedly pointed out the heavy losses that both sides have taken since Russia's invasion of Ukraine, which began in early 2022.
"This is the first time I feel like we see real desire on the Russian side to finish," the official said.

A138.text:
Verfahrene Lage am Persischen Golf Irankrieg laut Trump »effektiv vorüber« – Teheran spricht von »Fake News«
Wann ist wieder mit einem dauerhaften Frieden zwischen Iran und den USA zu rechnen, wann mit Entspannung für den Welthandel mit Öl und Treibstoff? US-Präsident Donald Trump sieht derzeit offenbar zumindest keinen Grund für weitere Kampfhandlungen gegen Iran.
Die militärische Auseinandersetzung mit Iran sei »effektiv vorüber«, so Trump nach einem Treffen mit dem katarischen Regierungschef Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani. »Wir halten den Status quo aufrecht, und das tun wir auf Drängen der Nachbarländer«, sagte der US-Präsident.
Katar tritt als ein Unterhändler in dem Konflikt auf. »Vor allem Katar, Saudi-Arabien, die Vereinigten Arabischen Emirate, Bahrain, Kuwait und andere würden den Status quo bevorzugen«, hatte Trump zuvor auf Truth Social mitgeteilt.
Die Seeblockade gegen Iran bleibe bestehen, allerdings seien keine neuen Angriffe geplant, sagte Trump. Er hoffe darauf, bald ein Friedensabkommen vereinbaren zu können. »Aber falls wir wieder eingreifen müssen, sind wir voll einsatzbereit und stehen bereit.« Das scheine derzeit aber unwahrscheinlich, hatte er zuvor auf Truth Social geschrieben.
Trump hatte neue Angriffe zuvor bereits als »höchst unwahrscheinlich« bezeichnet, das allerdings an Fortschritte in den Verhandlungen geknüpft. Die Aussagen laufen verschiedenen Medienberichten in den vergangenen Wochen zuwider, wonach Trump nach den US-Parlamentswahlen eine Wiederaufnahme groß angelegter Kampfhandlungen anordnen könnte.
Iran: USA sollen sich Bedingungen beugen
Zugleich hängt eine dauerhafte und breit angelegte Wiederaufnahme etwa der Frachtschifffahrt durch die Straße von Hormus auch von Teheran ab. Iran dürfte seinen militärischen Einfluss auf die wichtige Welthandelsroute auch in Zukunft geltend machen.
Der Chef des iranischen Sicherheitsrates, Mohsen Rezaee, ließ derweil wenig Kompromissbereitschaft durchblicken. Die USA sollten »aufhören, Fake News über imaginierte Verhandlungen zu produzieren«, so Rezaee laut der Nachrichtenagentur Reuters. Es sei »Zeit, sich den sieben Bedingungen zu beugen, die Iran wiederholt aufgestellt hat«. Es gilt allerdings als unwahrscheinlich, dass sich die USA auf die Forderungen einlassen.
Berichten zufolge sollen die USA unter anderem alle Kampfhandlungen gegen Iran und dessen Verbündete in der Region, wie die Hisbollah im Libanon, einstellen. Außerdem sollen die Seeblockade gegen iranische Häfen und Schiffe beendet, Sanktionen sowie das Verbot von Ölexporten aufgehoben und eingefrorene iranische Vermögenswerte freigegeben werden. Teheran verlangt demnach auch Reparationen für Kriegsschäden.

A154.text:
Ukraine, Russia and US return to talks in Abu Dhabi: What to expect?
November 10, 2026
A new round of trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraineand the United States are scheduled to take place in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday, months after a flurry of US-mediated peace talks earlier this year in January and February went nowhere.
When announcing the new trilateral talks last week, US special envoy Steve Witkoff said the discussions would focus on "post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has named security guarantees, an energy ceasefire, unblocking the Black Sea, extended prisoner exchanges, and preparations for a meeting of the leaders of Ukraine, the United States and Russia as his key topics.
Lawmaker Davyd Arakhamia, a member of Ukraine's delegation, told DW he was not expecting quick progress.
"I don't think there will be a breakthrough, after there was such a long break in the negotiation process," he said. "Simply the fact that trilateral talks are being resumed can be counted as a success."
Who is sitting at the table?
Witkoff will be joined by US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, real estate developer Jared Kushner, who serves as special envoy.
The Kremlin has sent Vladimir Medinsky, an aide to Russian President Vladimir Putin, to act as chief negotiator, along with a delegation including high-ranking Russian military and intelligence officials.
The Ukrainian delegation will be led by Rustem Umerov, head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service, along with Arakhamia, and diplomatic and military officials.
Europe joins in
Separate formats are planned with several European representatives.
These include Günter Sautter, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's foreign and security policy adviser, Emmanuel Bonne, head of the Elysee Palace's diplomatic service and Jonathan Powell, the UK's national security advisor, and Fabrizio Saggio, diplomatic adviser to Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.
Björn Seibert, Chief of Staff for the President of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, and Geoffrey van Leeuwen, Chief of Staff for NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte, will also attend.

U.S. President Donald Trump on Monday told reporters he believes the war in Iran “militarily is effectively over,“ suggesting that – at least for now – he’s not prepared to resume the bombardment that has devastated the Islamic Republic and caused reverberations across the global economy.
The President made a surprise visit to the White House briefing room after meeting earlier in the day with Qatar’s Prime Minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani.
“Iran militarily is effectively over,” Trump said. “We’re just keeping it the status quo.”
He added that Iran has been “decapitated” but said he is still looking to make sure there’s a long-term solution to ensuring that Iran’s nuclear program is defanged.
Trump should carry weight of Jan. 6 riots to ‘his grave,’ Biden writes in new memoir
It was some of Trump’s most definitive comments about moving away from his threat to resume strikes on Iran after the U.S. midterm elections had passed.
The President’s Republican Party lost both chambers of Congress to Democrats in last week’s elections. The elections were shadowed by dissatisfaction among the American electorate over the eight-month-old war, which has led to a surge in fuel prices that’s impacted nearly ever sector of the global economy.
Trump, over the course of the conflict, has repeatedly said he is on the cusp of ordering U.S. forces to escalate attacks if Iran’s leaders don’t quickly agree to U.S. terms to end the war, only to back down. In earlier cycles, he has also edged away with a last-minute declaration, sometimes at the behest of Gulf allies, that he’s going to give diplomacy more time.
In a posting on social media shortly before speaking to reporters, Trump once again asserted that Middle East allies – Qatar, Saudi Arabia, United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Kuwait and others – ”would prefer the status quo.“ Minutes later, in his exchange with reporters, he sought to assure war-weary Americans that there was “positive momentum” and that he saw a “good chance” that the war “could get ended.”
“They’re talking to us, and they’re talking very politely, And we’ll see what happens,” Trump said. He added, “The military action doesn’t seem to be a very necessary thing, but we’re locked and loaded, ready to go for any reason that changes.“
Trump, however, gave no hint of a drawdown of the thousands of U.S. troops who have been shifted to the waters off of Iran and maintain a naval blockade to stem the flow of Iranian oil into the global market.
“We’re keeping it going. We have the greatest military blockade ever,” Trump said.
Qatari officials last week presented proposals on Iran’s nuclear program, according to two Middle East government officials familiar with the matter who spoke on the condition of anonymity.
The White House declined to comment, though Trump last week alluded to continuing indirect talks with Tehran.
All the while, Tehran continues to insist on several concessions from the U.S., which Trump has declined in the past. Among the core demands Iran says must be met before engaging in nuclear talks: ending the U.S. blockade on Iran’s ports, lifting sanctions, unfreezing its assets, issuing compensation for war damage and ending hostilities throughout the region, including Israeli operations in Lebanon.
Earlier Monday, Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has come under fire over the conflict, said the next steps on the war are up to Trump, including the possibility of telling Iran: “Hey, we’re done, and we’re going to watch your nuclear material. You better not move it.”
The Defence Secretary has been one of the administration’s most prominent defenders of the war. Critics say the administration launched the war without proper authorization, violated the War Powers Resolution and subverted congressional war-declaring powers.
Republican Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky moved Monday to force a vote to impeach Hegseth, largely over his execution of the war.
