A35.text:
Russia and Ukraine hold US-backed talks after Trump says broad deal is possible
By Roula Rouhana
ABU DHABI, Nov 10 (Reuters) - Russian and Ukrainian officials met on Tuesday for their first US-brokered talks since February, after President Donald Trump suggested last week that a broad deal was possible on ending the war in Ukraine and guaranteeing security in Europe.
Russian state news agency RIA reported the start of what is scheduled to be two days of talks, in which Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are to mediate between the two warring sides.
More than 4-1/2 years after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and with Russian forces holding about a fifth of the country, Moscow and Kyiv remain far apart - despite Trump's optimism - on terms for a possible settlement.
The new American drive for a deal has galvanised European officials into pushing for a place at the table to seek an end to the continent's deadliest conflict since World War Two.
Before the start of the main meeting, Kyiv's chief negotiator, Rustem Umerov, said Ukrainian officials had met separately with European, NATO and EU representatives and the two American envoys.
"We are doing everything to ensure that Europe is a participant in the diplomatic process," Umerov said before the meeting.
France said there could be no lasting peace in Ukraine without addressing European security, and that this required the involvement of the Europeans.
Russia had made clear it did not see a place for Europeans at the meeting with the Ukrainians and Americans.
TRUMP SAYS A DEAL COULD COME SOON
On the eve of the talks, Trump said Washington was seeing a "very strong inclination" towards ending the war, and that both sides were "tired of fighting". After meeting privately with Russian President Vladimir Putin's envoy last week at the White House, Trump predicted that a peace deal could emerge soon.
Trump has frequently said an agreement to end Europe's deadliest conflict since World War Two was close, without a deal emerging. However, negotiations have picked up again in recent weeks after months in which Washington's attention was focused on the war in Iran.
Publicly, there has been no sign that Putin is willing to drop his insistence that Ukraine surrender the entire eastern region of Donbas before a peace deal can be struck.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy has staunchly refused to hand over land that his forces have died defending. Russian front-line advances have slowed to a virtual halt this year.
A source in the Russian delegation said Russia believed the main thrust of the talks would be trying to hammer out the key elements of a new post-war security framework for Europe.
On the eve of the negotiations, Zelenskiy said Ukraine's leverage in the talks was increasing as a result of its recent battlefield performance, which has included retaking some territory in Donetsk, a coal-mining area of the Donbas.
"Ukrainian forces are currently genuinely strengthening Ukraine's negotiating position," Zelenskiy said in his nightly video address on Monday. He said Russia was suffering "record losses" — a claim disputed by Moscow — and urged Washington to convince the Kremlin to end the war.
US negotiators believe that Zelenskiy and Putin may be willing to strike a compromise on the vital question of territory, each ceding a little, a US official told Reuters.
Under the proposed deal, Ukraine would get an end to the war, security guarantees and a roadmap to accession to the EU.
A senior Ukrainian official strongly denied that the government would consider any such concessions. The issue of territory could be discussed only at a leaders' level and only in the context of appropriate security guarantees for Ukraine, the official said.
(Additional reporting by Dan Flynn and Yuliia Dysa in Kyiv, Steve Holland in Washington and John Irish in Paris, Writing by Mark Trevelyan, Editing by Timothy Heritage)

A554.text:
Israel’s new Knesset will be sworn in on Tuesday, giving opposition politicians their first chance to take control of some levers of power, even as they struggle to form a new government to unseat Benjamin Netanyahu.
High on the agenda will be replacing the speaker, who wields immense influence by controlling the legislature’s agenda. The role is currently held by Amir Ohana, a close ally of Netanyahu.
Gadi Eisenkot, the former Israeli military chief who got the presidential mandate to try to form a coalition government at the weekend, may take the role himself, Israeli media reported on Monday.
The effort to wrest away control of the Knesset is significant enough that more than 160 top former security officials, including heads of the military, intelligence and police, warned that rightwing activists were planning to disrupt the day with violent attacks.
“Actors who oppose replacing the Knesset speaker intend to go to the Knesset on the day of the swearing-in ceremony and to prevent the MKs and their family members from entering the building,” a forum of retired commanders, the Democracy’s Protective Wall, warned in a letter to serving security chiefs.
“These same actors are encouraging tens of thousands of citizens who support their stance to come and to help them with their mission,” Ma’ariv newspaper quoted the letter saying.
If Eisenkot does not take the speaker role, opposition parties have agreed that someone from his Yashar party will be the nominee.
The opposition parties hold 67 seats in the 120-seat legislature, enough to install a consensus choice for speaker. All have described the current prime minister as a threat to the state and are keen to start moving against him, despite divides blocking the formation of a coalition.
But several of the Jewish-Israeli opposition parties in his “change” bloc have sworn not to sit with the Palestinian-led parties that hold over a quarter of the bloc’s seats, or even join a minority government that has their backing.
Eisenkot has vowed to broker a national emergency government, promising to achieve it with “creative and unconventional political acts”.
In a sign of challenges ahead, he effectively warned that some election promises would have to be broken to unseat Netanyahu.
“No one will be able to fulfil all the [campaign] promises they made, and all of us will need to compromise. That is also leadership, to know when to decide and set priorities,” he said.
There have been protests across Israel urging Jewish-Israeli opposition parties to put unseating Netanyahu ahead of a racist commitment to excluding Palestinian-led parties from government.
Palestinian citizens of Israel make up about 20% of Israel’s population and voted in unprecedented numbers this year, giving them 19 seats. Without them, the opposition bloc has fewer seats than Netanyahu’s diminished coalition.
Rightwing opposition leader Avigdor Lieberman has been trying to seek an alternative path to government through an alliance with ultra-Orthodox parties. They have long been Netanyahu allies but have been frustrated by his failure to deliver on the promise to pass broad military draft exemptions for their community into law. Lieberman has campaigned hard for universal conscription, but appears to prefer compromise on this issue to working with Palestinians.
“Has the End of Times arrived?” leading Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) journalist Arye Erlich wrote in a column for Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper.
“Has Avigdor Lieberman … the biggest persecutor of Haredim Israeli politics has seen in decades, suddenly come to believe that he can compromise on a military draft bill and sit in a coalition government alongside the Haredim?”
Even if Eisenkot does broker a coalition deal, he may delay announcing it until Netanyahu’s speaker has been replaced. Netanyahu is a master of political survival and last-minute deals, fracturing past coalitions by luring defectors into his own alliance.

Ukraine peace talks resume with 'some flexibility' by warring sides, US officials say
- Published
Trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine have begun in Abu Dhabi.
Although expectations for a breakthrough that ends Russia's full-scale war on Ukraine are low, US officials said yesterday that Moscow and Kyiv were privately showing "a little bit of flexibility" on the issue of who would control Ukraine's eastern regions in a postwar scenario.
Jared Kushner - Donald Trump's son-in-law and part of the US delegation alongside peace envoy Steve Witkoff - said the talks would be focused on addressing the "postwar security concerns" of both Russia and Ukraine.
"An important part of this process is encouraging all parties to begin thinking seriously about what comes after the war," Kushner wrote on X.
Ahead of the meeting, the two US envoys met Ukrainian and European and Nato officials in Abu Dhabi, and French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot was adamant that France, the UK and Germany "will indeed be in the meeting room".
European officials are wary of Russia trying to secure a deal with the US on future "collective security" without them, and Moscow and Kyiv's positions on ending the conflict are still far apart.
A key area of disagreement between the two involves Ukraine's eastern region of Donetsk, which is by now mostly occupied by Russia.
Moscow has demanded that Ukraine relinquish the parts of Donetsk which it still holds, while Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line to maintain control over those sections, which it says are crucial to its future security.
While neither side has budged on these demands, the US official speaking on the eve of the talks suggested that this was just the public stance and that Moscow and Kyiv had shown "a little bit of flexibility, privately".
However, he acknowledged that the issue would not be solved without discussions about a new "security architecture".
"They will not solve the Donetsk issue and the territorial issue until they know what the security architecture is going to be after the war," the official said. "And keep in mind, we're not going to be able to finalise one without the other."
For Ukraine, a post-war "security architecture" may include reassurance that allies will come to its aid if it's attacked again. For Russia, that could be its longstanding ambition to see Nato roll back from eastern Europe – which would be alarming to Europeans.
The framework being proposed includes security consultations and crisis communications hotlines, as well as "reciprocal de-escalation measures" between the two. The officials also floated the re-activation of the Nato-Russia Council that has been largely paused since 2022.
The last round of trilateral talks, held in Geneva in February, ended without a breakthrough. Soon after, the US-Israel war on Iran diverted Washington's attention from Ukraine, and no other discussions were held since.
Since then, European leaders - who have been largely excluded from peace talks – have pushed to be involved in the process amid concerns that decisions about the security of their continent would be made without them.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen urged on Monday to include Nato allies and EU members into any "meaningful discussions about Europe's security architecture". President Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly stated Kyiv wanted Europe to be part of the talks.
The US official said the Americans would propose moving into a multilateral format bringing the Europeans into the discussion. "Hopefully we'll get the Russians on board," the official said, while acknowledging that "the Russians have a bad taste in their mouth with the Europeans."
Since the start of his second term in office, US President Donald Trump – who once boasted he could end the war in Ukraine within a day – has spearheaded several rounds of talks to end the conflict, albeit with little success.

Iranian hackers like to send a message.
In 2023 a state-backed group interrupted TV streaming services in the United Arab Emirates to broadcast a deepfake report on the war in Gaza. In the same year, hackers affiliated with Iran displayed the slogan “down with Israel” on the screens of water-control equipment made by an Israeli firm.
Now France has attributed an attack on supermarket fridges to hackers operating under the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, a key branch of Iran’s military establishment.
There was no message this time, but the disruption made headlines around the world. Some refrigerators had their temperature turned up so high they caught fire. In the hours after the hack, supermarket employees dumped piles of perished meat and melted ice-cream into rubbish containers.
France’s foreign minister described it as an act of “unprecedented scale and unprecedented aggression” and promised “Europe-wide sanctions” would be imposed against those responsible.
It follows attacks on industrial freezers at an Israeli food production plant in May and a wave of freezer malfunctions that spoiled food at US military bases in August that are now reportedly being treated as a suspected hack. Those attacks have not been officially attributed to Iran, but the French announcement is the first to implicate the state in this type of hack.
Rafe Pilling, a senior director at Sophos, a cybersecurity firm, said the relatively unsophisticated nature of the attack – hackers used default passwords to access fridge controls – was in line with Iranian capabilities. “The attacks themselves were not particularly complex,” he said.
Pilling said there was now a presumption the French attacks and a wave of rogue defrosting hacks across Europe last week were linked.
Hostile cyber operations against the west tend to come from a vexatious quartet of China, Russia, Iran and North Korea. All have different aims and characteristics: China has focused on industrial espionage and mass data gathering, Russia on disrupting enemy infrastructure and spreading disinformation, and North Korea on hacking crypto exchanges because it needs money. Iran, according to Pilling, wants to put a shot across the bow of its enemies.
“In general Iran uses cyber-attacks to project power internationally and to signal their political displeasure with regional and international adversaries,” Pilling said.
The fridge hacks came as the UK’s national cybersecurity centre warned the country is in the “foothills” of a new level of cyber threat – and should expect a “huge rise” in the volume of incidents. The main concern is AI, a technology now capable of highlighting previously unforeseen flaws in IT systems and helping attackers plan and carry out attacks.
However, the underlying context of the fridge attacks is not AI but geopolitics. After all, the refrigeration system vulnerabilities were relatively easy to find and exploit. But a combination of groundbreaking technology and tense global relations makes for an alarming landscape.

A593.text:
The US military has reportedly evacuated aircraft from a second airbase in Britain after a threat from Iran.
Two US refuelling tankers that were using the RAF Mildenhall military base diverted to Germany on Monday morning, while several other tankers at the base were moved to Germany and other locations later in the day, according to the Wall Street Journal.
Washington withdrew its bombers from RAF Fairford airbase in September over a suspected Iran-linked security incident.
The precise nature of the threat to RAF Mildenhall remained under discussion among US officials, it was reported.
The cabinet minister Lucy Powell said the security of military bases in the UK was constantly under review. She told Sky News she could not comment on live operations, “but we’re constantly keeping the security of our bases under review and, as we’ve seen with other cases recently, we take firm and quick action where we need to”.
A Ministry of Defence spokesperson said: “We do not routinely comment on the activity of other nations. Aircraft and other assets move regularly according to operational requirements.”
The US had upgraded the security threat level at RAF Mildenhall and RAF Lakenheath, the report said, citing a US official familiar with the matter.
The base was placed under Force Protection Condition (FPCON) Charlie, which is the second-highest defensive threat level in the US Department of Defense’s security system and occurs when intelligence indicates a form of terrorist action is likely.
It is understood that, on the ground, there has been no specific threat against the RAF base. No arrests have been made, suggesting the threat seen by the US was more general.
A US Air Force spokesperson said: “US Air Force aircraft rotate between installations and operating locations for a variety of reasons, including training and real world requirements. US military aircraft are hosted in accordance with access, basing, and overflight agreements with our allies and partners. Due to operations security, we will not provide further information on movement of assets.”
Five men were arrested outside RAF Fairford airbase in Gloucestershire in September over a suspected plot to attack the base.
Two men, Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, and Nouman Essghir, 24, who were not among the men arrested at RAF Fairford, later appeared in court charged under the National Security Act 2023 in connection with the incident. Abdulkarim, from Westminster, was charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service, which police earlier said they believed to be Iran.
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said last month that the activity at RAF Fairford was likely to have been coordinated in Iran.
While Tehran’s ambassador to Britain has denied accusations it was involved in any plot against the airbase, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said in July that Fairford and any other bases used to launch attacks against Iran were legitimate targets.

A62.text:
Trump says more US attacks on Iran 'highly unlikely'
- Published
Donald Trump has said "Iran militarily is effectively over", and said that there is "positive momentum" behind negotiations to end the Middle East conflict.
"We're just keeping it the status quo," the US president said on Monday. "And we're doing that really at the behest of countries that are their neighbours."
Trump's comments came after he met the Qatari prime minister. Qatar is a US ally in the Gulf region, and one of Iran's neighbours, which has been a key mediator in efforts to end the war.
Addressing reporters in the White House press briefing room, Trump said that renewed US attacks on Iran were "highly unlikely" but that the US was "locked and loaded" should the circumstances change.
Iranian officials have repeatedly expressed doubts about Trump's prior comments about resolving the conflict.
This is not the first time that Trump has said the Iran war is "militarily" over, but the circumstances for him are different now.
The president has hinted at de-escalation in Iran after a bruising set of midterm election results for the Republicans last week, which senior figures including Vice-President JD Vance blamed on the Iran war.
Ahead of the midterms, Trump had said US forces conducted what he described as "minor strikes" on an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz. However, in an interview with 60 Minutes that aired on Sunday, the president said that he did not currently see "any reason" to escalate the conflict.
Responding to a question over why he would not officially declare an end to the war, Trump said that some of the Gulf allies could still face Iranian aggression.
"We have some great allies there and we have to make sure they're not hurt," he said, suggesting that the US naval blockade on Iranian ports was helping to make the region more secure.
Global oil prices, which have fallen sharply since the midterms, dipped further after Trump's comments.
On Tuesday afternoon in Asia, Brent crude was more than 1% lower at $91.50 (£52) while US-traded was down by 1.2% at $85.82.
Trump hosted Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdul Rahman Al Thani in the Oval Office earlier on Monday, saying they had an "excellent conversation" about negotiations to end the war.
In a post on X, the Qatari leader said he held "positive discussions" with Trump and Vance on "reaching a deal and bringing peace to the region".
Efforts to broker a peace between Washington and Tehran have largely been held indirectly through mediators since the war first broke out following joint US-Israeli strikes in February.
Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates are among the US's Gulf allies that have been hit by Iranian strikes over the course of the war, in addition to the threat of strikes that have led to major air travel disruptions in the region.
Post-election recriminations over the US war in Iran are already placing pressure on members of the Trump administration.
Republican congressman Thomas Massie launched a strong attack against Trump's Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday over the war in Iran, requesting a vote in the House of Representatives to impeach him.
Trump has backed Hegseth, who says he is "not worried" about the looming impeachment threats, calling Massie's effort a "sham".
While the move is unlikely to succeed with Republicans still in control of Congress until January, Democrats have expressed willingness to impeach Hegseth once the new session begins and they have control of both the House and the Senate.

Recent reporting noted that since last year, US intelligence reports had identified Alice Huang (no relation) as not only the exec for an AI compute company renting access to Nvidia GPUs, but also a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security.
In recent years, Nvidia has become a key part of the Trump administration’s AI push, a central figure in negotiations over potential Chinese access to cutting-edge AI hardware, and a company that has used its now $4 trillion-plus market cap to finance other AI companies, including the “neoclouds” like Coreweave who have been some of its biggest customers. So far, Nvidia and Jensen Huang have said that they have “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised,” but that hasn’t settled things as the investigation continues.
- What could China get from Jensen Huang? It’s difficult to overstate Nvidia’s power in today’s AI landscape. The company’s chips are the bedrock upon which advanced AI technology in the US is being built, and demand has consistently outpaced supply for years. Nvidia has also been an influential investor in a wide range of up-and-coming AI companies in recent years, with about $99 billion worth of equity investments in frontier AI labs, neoclouds, infrastructure companies, and more. Its chief executive has even become close with President Donald Trump. This is why, as both cofounder and longtime CEO of Nvidia, Jensen Huang would be a valuable target for a foreign adversary with sights on the American AI industry. Read Article >
- Here’s what Trump said he knew about Jensen Huang President Trump held a White House press briefing earlier today and responded to several questions about his knowledge of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Huang said this weekend that he had been “unfaithful” to his wife, and the company has opened an investigation into Huang. Recent articles from The New York Times indicated that Trump had been aware of a relationship between Huang and Alice Huang, the suspected spy, before information about it became public. In October, The New York Times reported that Trump had been briefed “roughly a year ago” on intelligence that Huang and the alleged spy, Alice Huang, had developed a close relationship, but he didn’t do anything with the information. Yesterday, the NYT reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio helped draft a memo to Trump officials about the relationship before Trump visited China in May. Read Article >

A89.text:
Business
Nvidia's shares slide as chip giant probes CEO Jensen Huang over spy claims
Internal probe follows media report that Huang had relationship with Chinese woman who allegedly shared info
Nvidia shares tumbled on Monday after an internal investigation into whether CEO Jensen Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort put his future at the AI chipmaker under scrutiny.
The internal probe followed a media report that Huang had a close relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who allegedly passed information to Beijing. Huang told Nvidia's employees that he had been unfaithful to his wife, without disclosing details of the relationship.
The investigation, announced on Sunday, has put a spotlight on Huang's future given Nvidia's status as the world's most valuable chipmaker and the CEO's role as the most prolific salesman of the AI boom.
The leather-jacketed Huang enjoys rock star status worldwide, particularly in Asia, where he often mingles freely with fans, taking selfies and signing autographs for his devoted followers.
He is Nvidia's fifth-largest shareholder with a roughly 3.6 per cent stake, according to LSEG data, and he keeps a tight grip on the company through an unusually flat structure in which dozens of executives report directly to him.
But unlike Meta Platforms or SpaceX, Nvidia has no dual-class shares that would give its co-founder majority voting control.
The fallout of the probe extended to South Korea, where Madison Huang, Huang's daughter and an Nvidia executive, cancelled a planned visit to Seoul for an Nvidia conference that was set to begin on Monday, according to companies she had been scheduled to meet.
Nvidia's shares tumbled about six per cent and hit their lowest intraday level since March 31.
"The market's probably telling you now this does no favours to the stock whatsoever in a time when there's a lot of conjecture as to the build-out of data centres," said Chris Weston, head of research at brokerage Pepperstone in Melbourne, Australia.
But Weston said he did not think Huang, whom he described as the "godfather of AI," would be replaced.
"If we genuinely thought he was going to step down … the stock would be down — it would be an absolute bloodbath, to be honest," he said.
Nvidia said its board has confidence in Huang. Some analysts said he has no natural successor within the company in case he decides to step down.
The New York Times reported last month that Huang had a relationship with Alice Huang, an unrelated former executive of Singapore-based company Megaspeed, who U.S. authorities investigated and concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset.
"The so-called Chinese spy narrative is purely a groundless accusation, slander, and a smear," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters in Beijing.
A screengrab from CTI video footage obtained Monday shows a woman identified by Reuters as Alice Huang, after comparison with a photograph obtained separately, attending a dinner with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at a restaurant in Taipei, Taiwan, on May 22, 2025. (CTI/Reuters)
Megaspeed did not respond immediately to a request for comment on Monday, a public holiday in Singapore.
Alice Huang did not respond to the New York Times last month when it first reported her relationship with Huang, and Reuters could not determine her location to seek comment on Monday.
Asia partners unaffected
Shares in Nvidia's key Asian chip suppliers rebounded on Monday after last week's selloff of AI-related stocks, with TSMC closing 4.7 per cent higher, while Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix ending up 0.6 per cent and 0.4 per cent, respectively.
Some prominent figures weighed in on Huang's admission. Billionaire investor Bill Ackman, founder of Pershing Square Capital Management, said on X the Nvidia CEO was an "incredible human," but if "indeed this is more than an affair, then it is obviously a real problem."
"I am hoping for a simple affair, not a risk to our national security," he said.
